articleSummary: Mpox (monkeypox) is a viral disease with two clades: Congo Basin (up to 10% mortality) and West African (about 1% mortality; the 2022 outbreak). There is no mpox-specific approved treatment; antivirals developed for smallpox may help, usually reserved for immunocompromised patients: cidofovir, brincidovir (Tembexa), and tecovirimat (Tpoxx). Incubation is 5–21 days; initial flu-like symptoms (fever, headache, muscle aches, lymphadenopathy, fatigue) precede a rash that begins on the face and spreads to the hands and feet. Transmission occurs through close contact with infected people or animals, including respiratory secretions, lesions, or contaminated materials; animal exposure includes bites, scratches, meat, or products. Pregnant individuals can pass the virus to a fetus. Diagnosis relies on PCR from lesion samples. Vaccines: JYNNEOS (two-dose, approved 2019; up to 85% effective; effective within four days of exposure) and ACAM2000 (single-dose). Mpox is typically self-limiting in 14–21 days, though severe disease and complications can occur, especially in children.

articleHeadline: In 1902, Hanoi paid people for rat tails to fight plague; more than 55 million tails were collected, but the rats were still alive
articleSummary: During 1902 in Hanoi, then French Indochina, plague-driven rat bounty paid one cent per rat tail; within a year, over 55 million tails submitted, yet many tailless rats remained alive, revealing that tails served as proof of kill, not proof of removal. Officials observed tailless rats still in sewer-linked streets, and rat catchers released animals after payment. The episode, part of the Third Plague Pandemic, is cited in a 2026 npj Biodiversity review (as of 2026-10-03) as an example of unintended outcomes from species bounty programs. The authors, analyzing 283 species across 449 programmes in 60 countries over eight centuries, note that financial rewards can increase participation but also drive fraud, poaching, or preservation of target species. Other cases include Britain’s grey squirrel bounty and discussions of the cobra effect; some schemes fail to reduce populations while altering incentives.

articleHeadline: Clean Chemistry, Hidden Germs: Ghana's Boreholes Reveal a Groundwater
articleSummary: Sixteen boreholes supplying domestic water in Segyemase, Juaso, and Nsuapemso in Ghana's Eastern Region appear chemically pristine (pH 5.38–7.29, conduct. ~173.5 μS/cm, TDS ~135 mg/L; fluoride below 1.5 mg/L). Yet microbiological testing found faecal coliforms and Escherichia coli in two boreholes, implying potential infection risk with an annual probability up to about 58% for the worst source. The study, published in Discover Geoscience, used an integrated framework combining hydrochemical characterization, six water quality/pollution indices, microbiological indicators, ecological risk diagnostics, and quantitative microbial risk assessment; samples were collected September 2022 during the late wet season and analyzed at CSIR-WRI Accra per APHA methods. Hydrochemistry indicates groundwater from Proterozoic Birimian rocks dominated by carbonate dissolution and silicate weathering, with pH strongly linked to bicarbonate (r=0.97) and iron to manganese (r=0.90). Composite indices correlated highly; trace metals pollution index showed a more complex story.

articleHeadline: Bloodstream infections in children: 73% of Klebsiella isolates are resistant to meropenem.
articleSummary: Meropenem-resistant bloodstream infections in children at Yangon Children's Hospital, Myanmar, based on a study published Oct 3, 2026 in Scientific Reports, covering Aug 2023–Jul 2025. Among 4,263 pediatric blood samples (median age 228 days; 765 positive), 160 isolates across five species were analyzed, led by Klebsiella pneumoniae (85 isolates, 53.1%). Overall, 82.5% of the isolates were resistant to at least one antibiotic per WHO GLASS. Meropenem resistance was 72.9% among K. pneumoniae and 38.5% among Escherichia coli. The presence of NDM metallo-beta-lactamase—an enzyme that inactivates many beta-lactams—was detected by rapid testing in 47% of 134 Gram-negative isolates; among 71 meropenem-resistant isolates, 88.7% carried NDM. Authors emphasize rapid diagnostics, antibiograms, infection control, and prudent antibiotic use to guide therapy, noting the findings are from a single pediatric hospital and contextualized within global resistance trends reported by WHO.
